title: MEA confirms Arunachal talks with China, eyes report of satellite aid to Pakistan
dek: The MEA said commanders discussed border management and 'outstanding issues' on the LAC in the eastern sector. No agreement has been announced, and Beijing has not commented.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
Indian and Chinese military commanders have held two more rounds of talks on the Line of Actual Control in Arunachal Pradesh, aimed at drafting rules of engagement and preventing clashes between patrols before winter snow closes several patrolling routes, according to reports published on Sunday and Monday. The talks, held over about 10 days after Diwali at the border personnel meeting point at Wacha, north of Kibithoo in Anjaw district, have ended for now, reports said, citing unnamed officials.

The Ministry of External Affairs confirmed the talks on Wednesday, 25 November, saying a meeting of senior military commanders "was held in the eastern sector recently" and focused on "improving border management as well as addressing outstanding issues along the LAC". China's foreign ministry has not commented. The talks follow a Corps Commander-level meeting at the same venue on 6 to 8 September, and come after friction this summer near Taksing in Upper Subansiri district, where, according to reports, the Indian Army took a firm stand against positions adopted by Chinese troops.

## What the talks covered

The Indian delegation was led by Lt Gen Girish Kalia, who commands the Army's 3 Corps, headquartered at Dimapur in Nagaland, and included an official from the Ministry of External Affairs, according to reports. 3 Corps is responsible for a large part of the 1,140 km stretch of the LAC in Arunachal Pradesh. The Chinese side was led by his counterpart; reports did not name the Chinese officers.

The agenda had three parts, reports said: rules of engagement for the two armies, ways of stopping patrols from running into each other, and keeping communication channels open between local commanders. No agreement has been announced.

## What the MEA said

At his briefing in New Delhi on Wednesday, the ministry's spokesperson, Randhir Jaiswal, said: "India and China engage regularly through diplomatic and military mechanisms." He said such interactions aim at "maintaining peace and tranquillity in the border areas and preventing any escalation", according to reports. He did not say whether any agreement had been reached, and none has been made public.

Mr Jaiswal was also asked about a report that Pakistan may have used Chinese satellite data to track Indian troop movements and military installations during Operation Sindoor in May 2025. "We have seen some media reports on this particular issue," he said, adding that India would "closely follow the developments which may have a bearing on our security interest" and "take appropriate measures", according to reports. Neither Beijing nor Islamabad has commented on that report.

The question points to a wider risk for India: China is Pakistan's main arms supplier, and any sharing of Chinese surveillance data during a conflict would mean India faces the two neighbours' capabilities in combination, not separately. That concern sits alongside the eastern-sector friction the commanders were trying to manage.

## Why it matters

Unlike eastern Ladakh, where the two sides agreed on patrolling arrangements in October 2024 after the 2020 standoff, the eastern sector has no settled arrangement for where each side patrols. India treats the McMahon Line, drawn under the 1914 Simla Convention between British India and Tibet, as the boundary. China does not recognise it and claims most of Arunachal Pradesh as "southern Tibet". Because each side perceives the LAC differently, patrols regularly come face to face.

India's stated position, set out by the Ministry of External Affairs, is that the situation along the LAC "is periodically disturbed when Chinese forces deviate from established patrolling patterns", that peace in the border areas is essential for the wider relationship, and that "India does not accept any unilateral attempt to alter the status quo", according to reports. Beijing has made no public comment on these rounds.

Those on the ground describe continuing friction. Shatrujeet Kapur, a former director general of the Indo-Tibetan Border Police, said at an ITBP event in Alwar, Rajasthan, that troops from the two countries had come face to face at several points along the Arunachal frontier and that confrontations were continuing, according to reports. Arunachal Pradesh Chief Minister Pema Khandu has called the situation normal for an undefined boundary, but said: "Transgression has definitely happened. It continues to happen."

## The risks for India

Any clash in the eastern sector would put at risk the slow thaw in relations since the 2024 Ladakh agreement, including the resumption of direct flights and visa services. The eastern sector is also where China is building a giant hydropower project on the Yarlung Tsangpo, the river that becomes the Brahmaputra, just north of Arunachal Pradesh, and where both sides have expanded roads, villages and airstrips close to the LAC. India is adding border units of its own: the ITBP's new "Shaurya" platoons have been given specialised training for high-altitude operations, reports said. For north Bengal, the region's road and rail links through the Siliguri Corridor carry most of the troops and supplies that reach the eastern front.

## What happens next

National Security Adviser Ajit Doval and Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi, the two countries' special representatives on the boundary question, met in Beijing in August. No date has been announced for their next meeting or for another round of commanders' talks. Snowfall in the coming weeks is expected to close several high passes and reduce patrolling until spring.
